lessons.title: Developing an Irrigation Schedule
lessons.body: An irrigation schedule tells you when to irrigate and how much water to apply. Without one, you risk overwatering (wasting water, leaching nutrients) or underwatering (stressing crops, reducing yields). Start by knowing your soil type. Sandy soils hold little water and need frequent, small applicationsâmaybe every 2-3 days. Clay soils hold more but drain slowly; irrigate every 5-7 days. Loam is ideal: every 3-4 days. Next, know your crop's root depth and critical growth stages. For example, maize needs more water during tasseling and silking. Tomatoes peak during flowering and fruit fill. A simple schedule: check soil moisture by hand (dig 10 cm, squeeze a handfulâif it crumbles, it's dry; if it forms a ball, it's moist). If dry, irrigate until the top 30 cm is wet. For a typical 1-hectare vegetable plot in Kenya, you might apply 20-30 mm per irrigation (20-30 litres per square metre) every 3 days. Use a rain gauge or a simple tin can to measure how much water you apply. If you have a 200-litre drum and a watering can, you can calculate: 1 mm of water = 1 litre per square metre. So 20 mm = 20 litres per square metre. For a 10 m x 10 m plot (100 mÂ²), you need 2000 litres. That's 10 drums. Adjust based on rainfall: if it rains 10 mm, skip that day's irrigation. Write your schedule on a calendar or phone reminder. Review weeklyâcrops change, weather changes. A good schedule saves water, time, and money.

lessons.title: Using Evapotranspiration Data for Scheduling
lessons.body: Evapotranspiration (ET) is the combined water lost from soil evaporation and plant transpiration. Knowing ET helps you replace exactly what the crop uses. In Africa, many weather stations and online tools provide ET data. For example, the FAO's AquaCrop or the online tool 'CropWat' (free from FAO) can estimate ET for your location. But you don't need a computer. A simple pan evaporimeterâa shallow pan of water exposed to sunâcan give you a rough ET estimate. Place a pan (like a frying pan) in an open area, fill with water, and measure daily loss. Pan evaporation is usually 1.2 to 1.5 times higher than crop ET. So if the pan loses 8 mm, your crop might use about 6 mm. For a maize field at flowering, daily ET might be 5-7 mm in hot, dry conditions. That means you need to apply 5-7 litres per square metre per day. If you irrigate every 3 days, apply 15-21 mm. For a 100 mÂ² plot, that's 1500-2100 litres. But ET varies with crop stage: young seedlings use 1-2 mm/day, while full canopy uses 5-8 mm/day. Use a simple table: for leafy vegetables, ET is about 3-5 mm/day; for tomatoes, 4-6 mm/day; for maize, 5-7 mm/day. Check local weather forecastsâif a heatwave is coming, increase water. If cloudy and cool, reduce. Many African farmers use the 'crop coefficient' method: ETc = ETo x Kc. ETo is reference ET (from a weather station or pan), and Kc is crop coefficient (e.g., 0.4 for seedling, 1.1 for mid-season maize). You can find Kc values in FAO-56. Start with these numbers, then adjust by watching your plantsâif leaves wilt in the afternoon, you're behind. Keep a simple notebook: date, pan reading, crop stage, water applied. After a season, you'll know your farm's pattern.

lessons.title: Simple Tools for Scheduling: Tensiometers and Apps
lessons.body: You don't need expensive equipment to schedule irrigation. Two practical tools are tensiometers and smartphone apps. A tensiometer is a sealed tube with a ceramic tip and a vacuum gauge. You bury the tip at root depth (e.g., 20 cm for vegetables). When soil is wet, the gauge reads low (0-10 centibars). As soil dries, the reading rises. For most vegetables, irrigate when the gauge reads 30-40 centibars; for maize, 50-60 centibars. Tensiometers cost about $50-100 and last several seasons. In Africa, you can find them at agricultural supply stores in Nairobi, Lagos, or Accra. If you can't afford one, use a simple 'gypsum block' or even a 'feel method': dig 10 cm, squeeze soilâif it holds together but breaks when poked, it's time to irrigate. For apps, 'FAO WaPOR' provides free satellite ET data for Africa. 'CropWat' (offline) helps calculate water needs. 'IrriSAT' (Australia) but works globally if you input coordinates. 'AgriApp' or 'FarmBeats' are used in East Africa. Many apps use your phone's GPS to get weather and ET. For example, 'Rain Bird' app helps schedule based on crop and soil. But beware: apps need internet and data. A simpler tool: a 'watermark' sensor (granular matrix) that you read with a handheld meterâcosts about $30. Or a 'tensiometer' with a dial. For a smallholder, a $20 'soil moisture meter' (capacitance type) can be stuck in the soil and gives a reading 1-10. Calibrate it: when soil is dry, reading is low; when wet, high. Use it daily at 20 cm depth. Combine tools: a tensiometer at 20 cm and a simple rain gauge. Record readings. After a few weeks, you'll see patterns. Remember, tools are guidesâyour eyes and hands are still the best. If plants look healthy and soil is moist, you're doing well.

lessons.title: Deficit Irrigation Strategies for Water Scarcity
lessons.body: When water is scarce, you can't keep soil at full moisture all the time. Deficit irrigation means deliberately applying less water than the crop's full requirement, accepting some yield reduction but saving water. The key is to target drought-tolerant stages. For many crops, flowering and grain filling are criticalâdon't stress then. But vegetative stages can tolerate some stress. For example, maize can tolerate 50% water deficit during vegetative growth (before tasseling) with little yield loss. Tomatoes can tolerate deficit during early vegetative stage, but not during flowering. A common strategy: 'regulated deficit irrigation' (RDI). For fruit trees like mango, apply 50-70% of full ET during fruit set, then full water during fruit sizing. For vegetables, use 'partial root-zone drying' (PRD): water only one side of the plant's root zone, alternating sides every 10-14 days. This saves 30-50% water while maintaining yield. In Africa, PRD works well for tomatoes, peppers, and maize. Another method: 'skip irrigation'âif you normally irrigate every 3 days, skip one day when soil is still moist. Use a tensiometer: allow readings to reach 60-70 centibars before irrigating, instead of 30-40. But watch for wilting. If leaves roll or droop in early morning, you've gone too far. Mulching helps: a 5 cm layer of dry grass or crop residues reduces evaporation by 30-50%, so deficit irrigation is less risky. Also, water at dawn or dusk to reduce evaporation. For a 1-hectare plot, deficit irrigation might save 1000-2000 cubic metres per season. But don't deficit irrigate young seedlings or during floweringâthat can kill the crop. Start with a small trial: divide your field into two, apply full water on one half, deficit on the other, and compare yields. Many African farmers have found that 70% of full water gives 90% of yieldâa good trade when water is short.

lessons.title: Monitoring and Adjusting for Weather Variability
lessons.body: Weather in Africa is unpredictable. A week of hot, dry winds can dry soil fast; a sudden downpour can waterlog. You must monitor and adjust. Start with a simple rain gaugeâa straight-sided tin can (like a baked bean can) placed in an open area. Measure rainfall daily at the same time. If you get 10 mm of rain, that's 10 litres per square metre. Subtract that from your irrigation requirement. For example, if your crop needs 20 mm and it rained 10 mm, irrigate only 10 mm. Also, watch temperature and wind. On hot days (above 35Â°C), ET increases by 20-30%. On windy days, more water evaporates. Use a simple thermometer and a windsock (a piece of cloth on a stick) to gauge. If it's very hot and windy, irrigate more frequentlyâmaybe every 2 days instead of 3. If cloudy and cool, stretch to 4-5 days. Keep a daily log: date, rainfall, max temp, wind, irrigation applied. After a season, you'll see patterns. For example, in the Sahel, the rainy season may bring 5 mm one day, then none for a week. In East Africa, short rains can be intense. Adjust by checking soil moisture: dig 10 cm, squeeze. If it's dry, irrigate even if you irrigated yesterday. If it's wet, wait. Also, watch for signs of waterlogging: yellowing leaves, wilting despite wet soil. That means too much waterâstop irrigating and improve drainage. Use a simple 'checkbook' method: keep a water balance. Start with soil at field capacity (full). Each day, subtract ET (e.g., 5 mm) and add rainfall. When the balance drops to 50% of available water, irrigate to refill. For a loam soil, available water might be 150 mm per metre depth. So for 30 cm root zone, 45 mm available. Irrigate when 22 mm remains. This method works with just a rain gauge and a thermometer. Adjust weekly based on forecastâif rain is predicted, skip irrigation. If a heatwave is coming, pre-irrigate. Being flexible is key.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Efficient Water Use
lessons.body: Keeping records is the simplest way to improve water efficiency. Without records, you guess. With records, you learn. Start a notebook or a simple spreadsheet on your phone. Record: date, crop, growth stage, irrigation method (drip, sprinkler, furrow), amount of water applied (in mm or litres), duration, rainfall (mm), and any observations (wilting, pests, etc.). Also record soil moisture readings if you use a tensiometer or meter. For example: '15 May 2025, tomatoes, flowering, drip, 20 mm, 2 hours, rain 0 mm, tensiometer 35 cb.' After a few weeks, you'll see how much water you actually use. Calculate water productivity: kilograms of yield per cubic metre of water. For a 1-hectare tomato field yielding 20 tonnes with 6000 mÂ³ water, that's 3.3 kg/mÂ³. If you can get 25 tonnes with 5000 mÂ³, that's 5 kg/mÂ³âbetter. Use records to compare seasons. Did you overwater in a wet year? Did you underwater in a dry year? Adjust next season. Also, record costs: pump fuel, labour, maintenance. This helps you see if deficit irrigation saves money. For smallholders, a simple 'water diary' works. Use a calendar: mark each irrigation day with a tick and amount. At the end of the month, count ticks. If you irrigated 10 times with 20 mm each, that's 200 mm. Compare to crop requirement (e.g., 500 mm for maize). If you're below, you might be deficit irrigatingâcheck yields. If above, you're wasting water. Share records with neighboursâthey may have insights. In Kenya, farmer groups use 'record books' to track water use and share tips. You can also use a mobile app like 'FarmLogs' or 'AgriTracker' to log. But paper is fine. The key is consistency. Even a simple tally on a wall chart helps. After one season, you'll know your farm's water needs precisely. That knowledge is powerâit saves water, money, and increases resilience to drought.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an irrigation schedule?
options: A) To decide when and how much to irrigate
B) To increase crop yield without water
quiz.explanation: An irrigation schedule guides timing and amount of water application to avoid over- or under-watering.

quiz.q: For a sandy soil, how often should you typically irrigate?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils hold little water, so frequent small applications are needed.

quiz.q: If 1 mm of water falls on 1 square metre, how many litres is that?
quiz.explanation: 1 mm of water over 1 mÂ² equals 1 litre.

quiz.q: What does ET stand for in irrigation?
quiz.explanation: ET is the combined water loss from soil evaporation and plant transpiration.

quiz.q: How much higher is pan evaporation compared to crop ET?
quiz.explanation: Pan evaporation is typically 1.2 to 1.5 times higher than crop ET.

quiz.q: For maize at flowering, what is a typical daily ET in hot, dry conditions?
quiz.explanation: Maize at flowering uses about 5-7 mm per day in hot, dry weather.

quiz.q: What is the crop coefficient (Kc) used for?
options: A) To adjust reference ET to crop-specific ET
quiz.explanation: Kc multiplies reference ET to get crop ET (ETc = ETo x Kc).

quiz.q: What does a tensiometer measure?
quiz.explanation: A tensiometer measures how tightly soil holds water (moisture tension).

quiz.q: For most vegetables, at what tensiometer reading should you irrigate?
quiz.explanation: Vegetables typically need irrigation when tension reaches 30-40 centibars.

quiz.q: Which app provides free satellite ET data for Africa?
quiz.explanation: FAO WaPOR offers free satellite-based ET data for Africa.

quiz.q: What is deficit irrigation?
options: A) Applying less water than full crop requirement
B) Applying more water than needed
quiz.explanation: Deficit irrigation deliberately applies less water, accepting some yield reduction to save water.

quiz.q: During which stage should you avoid deficit irrigation for maize?
quiz.explanation: Maize is most sensitive to water stress during tasseling and silking.

quiz.q: What is partial root-zone drying (PRD)?
options: A) Watering only one side of the root zone, alternating sides
B) Drying the entire root zone
quiz.explanation: PRD involves alternating irrigation on one side of the plant to save water.

quiz.q: How much water can mulching save by reducing evaporation?
quiz.explanation: A 5 cm mulch layer can reduce evaporation by 30-50%.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool to measure rainfall?
quiz.explanation: A straight-sided tin can acts as a simple rain gauge.

quiz.q: If your crop needs 20 mm and it rained 10 mm, how much should you irrigate?
quiz.explanation: Subtract rainfall from crop requirement: 20 mm - 10 mm = 10 mm.

quiz.q: On a hot, windy day, how does ET change?
quiz.explanation: Hot, windy conditions increase evapotranspiration by about 20-30%.

quiz.q: What does the 'checkbook' method for irrigation involve?
options: A) Keeping a water balance of ET and rainfall
B) Writing checks to pay for water
C) Using a checkbook to measure soil
D) Counting the number of irrigations
quiz.explanation: The checkbook method tracks soil moisture by subtracting ET and adding rainfall.

quiz.q: What is water productivity?
options: A) Yield per unit of water used
C) Cost of water per litre
D) Number of irrigations per season
quiz.explanation: Water productivity measures crop yield per cubic metre of water.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for irrigation?
options: A) It helps identify patterns and improve efficiency
B) It is required by law
C) It replaces the need for irrigation
quiz.explanation: Records show how much water was used and help adjust for better efficiency.

quiz.q: What should you record in a water diary?
options: A) Date, crop, water applied, rainfall
quiz.explanation: A water diary should include date, crop, amount applied, and rainfall.

quiz.q: How can you calculate water productivity?
options: A) Divide yield by water used
B) Multiply yield by water used
C) Add yield and water used
D) Subtract water used from yield
quiz.explanation: Water productivity = yield (kg) / water used (mÂ³).

quiz.q: What is a sign of over-irrigation?
options: A) Yellowing leaves and wilting despite wet soil
quiz.explanation: Waterlogging causes yellowing and wilting even when soil is wet.

quiz.q: What is the feel method for checking soil moisture?
options: A) Squeezing a handful of soil to see if it forms a ball
quiz.explanation: The feel method involves squeezing soil to estimate moisture content.

quiz.q: Which of these is a simple tool for scheduling irrigation?
quiz.explanation: A tensiometer measures soil moisture tension to guide irrigation timing.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of using a tensiometer over a calendar schedule?
options: A) It measures actual soil moisture, not just time
B) It is cheaper than a calendar
quiz.explanation: A tensiometer gives real-time soil moisture data, allowing more precise irrigation.

quiz.q: For a loam soil, what is a typical available water capacity per metre depth?
quiz.explanation: Loam soils typically hold about 150 mm of available water per metre depth.

quiz.q: When should you irrigate based on the checkbook method?
options: A) When soil moisture drops to 50% of available water
quiz.explanation: Irrigate when the water balance reaches 50% of available water to avoid stress.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of deficit irrigation?
options: A) Saves water with minimal yield loss
quiz.explanation: Deficit irrigation saves water while often maintaining acceptable yields.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid deficit irrigation during flowering?
options: A) It can severely reduce yield
B) It saves too much water
quiz.explanation: Flowering is a critical stage where water stress can drastically cut yield.
